Went quiet at "drowned stone", said folk who dream of lights go to Wren, the healer, and that the lights have not been seen from the landing for years but the cutters still won't cut on the Isle. His dog is a big grey hound named Edda's Rope (called Rope).

entries.text: notebook: updated Pim Tarr

The man's eyes go to the pole in your hand, then to your boots, then to the coppers. He takes the coins the way a ferryman does, without counting them. "Tar's mine," he says. "I do it every spring. Most don't notice." He nods at the stern pole. "Take the stern, then. She pulls left on the ebb, so lean into it."

The crossing is good work. The punt answers your pole well, and the rope hums under his hands. The water is black, slow and cold, and the reeds close in on both sides. He doesn't speak until the middle, where the channel is deepest.

"Pim," he says. "Pim Tarr. That's Rope on the step. The village is Reedholm." He gives you a sidelong look. "You said drowned stone and lights."

He lets the pole drag a moment.

"I was ten when the lights came. I'm not saying anything about them. But folk don't come asking about a stone, not unless they've seen it, and nobody has seen it who didn't cross the water to the Isle." He starts poling again. "The lights haven't shown from the landing in years. The cutters still won't cut reed on the Isle. If you've dreamed it, you want Wren. She keeps the healer's house at the landing. She's the one folk go to when something's wrong in the night. Fair warning, she isn't kind. She's good, though."

The far bank comes up out of the dusk, a plank landing and a stilted walk running into the reeds, with yellow windows glowing on pilings and a bell hanging silent from a post. It's a little past six. You're at full health with all your slots, and the drizzle is thickening to rain again.

What does Tamsin do?

His dog is named Eel. He says the green-white lights came back this autumn after years of quiet.

entries.text: notebook: updated Pim Tarr

The man looks at the coppers, then at your hands, and the wariness in his face eases a notch. "Tarr. Pim Tarr. I tar it myself, every spring." He takes one copper and pushes the other back. "Ferrier's rate is one. And yes, I'll take the second pair of hands. The current at the middle bites."

You pole the punt across together, with him on the rope and you on the stern, and he watches how you set your feet and read the water. Halfway over the current does bite, a slow black pull from the north. You lean into it without being told, and he says nothing, but he nods once. The dog pads aboard and sits between you like a passenger. Its name is Eel.

On the far bank he lights your lantern from his own, then stands looking at the dark reeds rather than at you. "That village is Reedholm, half a day on by the bank track. You'll not walk it tonight. The track floods at the low places after rain." He pauses. "Drowned stone. Lights. Who sent you?"

You say no one, only a dream. Pim is quiet so long that Eel looks up at him. "They went away when I was a boy," he says at last. "Years of quiet. This autumn they're back, low over the Hollow Isle, a mile out from Reedholm. The cutters keep off it. If you want to know what they are, ask Wren. She keeps the healer's house at Reedholm. She's the one who knows the old story, and she'll not thank you for guessing. She's sharp." He glances at your pole. "There's a dry bench in my hut and stew in the pot, if you want it. I'll not charge for that."

It's six past six on Day 1. You're at 24 of 24 hit points with all your slots, on the far bank of the Black Ford with a lit lantern, a grey dog at your knee, and the fen going dark around you.

Wren is quiet a long moment, and the amulet turns in her fingers. "A child drowned in the fen," she says. "Every family here has lost one, one way or another. I'd have to think which." She frowns. "Old Ode would know. She's gone to her bed, but she remembers everything older than I am."

You don't wait. You take Wren's lamp and walk the Long House's landing posts, running your thumb over the old wood. Investigation (21): on the third post, low down where a child could reach, half hidden under years of tar, someone has cut a name with a knife. It reads "WICK-ANNIS", with the picture of a candle beside it, drawn the way a six-year-old draws one, a stick with a flame on top. The cuts are deep and weathered, forty years old at least.

Wren reads it over your shoulder, and her face changes. "Annis," she says slowly. "Ode told me once. A little girl who went out at dusk to meet her father's skiff with a candle, so he'd see the landing. The fog came down. They found the candle, never her." She swallows. "I'd forgotten. time: 15 minutes later: Day 1, 8:25 PM

You say it quietly: it wasn't hunting the children, it was looking for a light that was hers once. Then you ask who in Reedholm lost a child to the fen.

Wren's face doesn't change. Insight (a natural 20, and a good one): you see what she is working not to show. She isn't surprised by the question. She has been waiting for someone to ask it.

"Come," she says, and takes the lamp. She leads you out to the back walk and kneels at the third stilt from the door. Low down, almost under the waterline's old stain, a name is cut in a child's shaky letters, with a later hand deepening them: LINNET.

"Linnet Rush," Wren says. "Ode's little sister. She was six. Ode was twelve. She fell from the west walk at dusk, chasing a candle someone had set on the boards. They never found her." She touches the carving. "Ode has lit a stub on that walk every year since, on the night it happened. She thinks nobody knows. I've watched her do it for years and kept my mouth shut."

Then she says the part she hasn't told anyone. She lifts Edda's amulet off her chest. "This goes warm in my hand when the small one is near. Tonight, when you spoke under the floor, it was warm as bread. It goes cold as a grave stone when I look toward the three on the Isle. I don't know what that means. I've been afraid to find out." She looks at you, and for the first time the flatness cracks a little. "I think the child is the only one of them that isn't hungry."

So there are two kinds of light out there: one that waits, and three that don't. And the children's game has been lighting candles for both.

It's twenty-five past eight. You have one 1st-level slot, two 2nd-level slots and 24 of 24 hit points. Ode Rush sleeps in her house at the far end of the walks, and she has no idea what you now know.
